enduring_issues_card.title: THE SIX UMBRELLAS
enduring_issues_card.intro: Every enduring issue fits under one of these six. Spot the umbrella fast. Then name the exact issue underneath it, and explain it.

umbrellas.name: POWER & ITS ABUSE
umbrellas.line: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.
umbrellas.issues_to_name: Abuse of Power · Imperialism · Human Rights Violations · Inequality

umbrellas.name: CONFLICT
umbrellas.line: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

umbrellas.name: IDENTITY & NATIONALISM
umbrellas.line: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

umbrellas.name: WEALTH & RESOURCES
umbrellas.line: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

umbrellas.name: TECHNOLOGY & ENVIRONMENT
umbrellas.line: What new tools let people do, and what they cost the world around them.
umbrellas.issues_to_name: Scientific and Technological Change · Environmental Crisis

umbrellas.name: A CONNECTED WORLD
umbrellas.line: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

close: On the essay, write the exact issue, not the umbrella: “Human Rights Violations,” not “Power & Its Abuse.”
Then EXPLAIN IT: define the problem in one sentence, and show where a document shows it.

documents.label: Unit 10.1 · Document 4
documents.title: Edict of 1635 Ordering the Closing of Japan
documents.source: Source: David John Lu, Sources of Japanese History, McGraw-Hill, from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005
documents.text:
• Japanese ships are strictly forbidden to leave for foreign countries.
• No Japanese is permitted to go abroad. If there is anyone who attempts to do so secretly, he must be executed. The ship so involved must be impounded and its owner arrested, and the matter must be reported to the higher authority.
• If any Japanese returns from overseas after residing there, he must be put to death. . . .
• Any informer revealing the whereabouts of the followers of padres (Christians) must be rewarded accordingly. If anyone reveals the whereabouts of a high ranking padre, he must be given one hundred pieces of silver. For those of lower ranks, depending on the deed, the reward must be set accordingly. . . .

documents.label: Unit 10.2 · Casefile B · Document 6
documents.title: About the Law of Suspects: a historians' summary
documents.source: Source: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity: Exploring the French Revolution (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media / American Social History Project) (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2015
documents.text: “This law, passed on 17 September 1793 [by Robespierre and the National Convention], authorized the creation of revolutionary tribunals to try those suspected of treason against the Republic and to punish those convicted with death. This legislation in effect made the penal justice system into the enforcement arm of the revolutionary government, which would now set as its primary responsibility not only the maintenance of public order but also the much more difficult and controversial task of identifying internal enemies of the Republic -- such as “profiteers” who violated the Maximum [decree to fix prices] -- and then removing them from the citizenry, where they might subvert [sabotage] the general will....”

pieces.text: In 1635, Japan's Tokugawa government was shutting the country off from the world, and in 1793, France's revolutionary government was at war and hunting for enemies at home.
Document 4 shows this when the Tokugawa government orders that any Japanese who returns from overseas “must be put to death.”
This matters because both governments turned their power on their own people, and it happened again 158 years later on another continent.

documents.label: Unit 10.1 · Document 2
documents.title: Aurangzeb and religious toleration
documents.source: Source: Donald J. Johnson et al., Through Indian Eyes, Apex Press, 1999 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2026
documents.text: Unfortunately, the last great Moghul [Mughal] ruler, Aurangzeb, opposed religious toleration. A devout Muslim and a Puritan in his habits, Aurangzeb dismissed the court musicians, artists, and historians. He discouraged poets, who “dealt in falsehood”; banned history, which “gave rise to feelings of undue pride”; and suppressed drinking and gambling. His military campaigns drained his resources. He also dismissed the Hindu clerks in his service and reimposed a poll tax on all “unbelievers.” These oppressive measures against the Hindus were perhaps the most destructive acts of his reign, for memories of Aurangzeb’s oppressive rule lingered in the minds of Hindu Indians for generations. By his death in 1707, the Moghul Empire was on the edge of ruin. The British came to fill the power vacuum.

documents.label: Unit 10.2 · Casefile A · Document 8
documents.title: Two voices from 1789: the slave trade
documents.source: Source: William Wilberforce, speech to the House of Commons, May 1789, in Cobbett, Parliamentary History of England, vol. 28 (adapted)
documents.text: “I confess to you sir, so enormous so dreadful, so irremediable [impossible to fix] did its wickedness appear that my own mind was completely made up for the abolition. A trade founded in iniquity [wrongdoing] . . . must be abolished . . . let the consequences be what they would, I from this time determined that I would never rest till I had effected [achieved] its abolition.”
documents.source_2: Source: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, London, 1794 edition (adapted), via OER Project
documents.text_2: “I now saw myself deprived [robbed] of all chance of returning to my native country . . . . I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation [greeting] in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life . . . . I became so sick and low that I was not able to eat . . . . I inquired [asked] of them what was to be done with us? They gave me to understand we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”
